# A Brief History of the Bicycle

The bicycle grew out of a long human quest for faster, more efficient personal transport, and its story is one of gradual refinement rather than a single invention. Its earliest ancestor appeared in 1817, when Karl Drais, a German baron and civil servant, built a two-wheeled, steerable machine that riders propelled by pushing their feet against the ground. Known as the *Laufmaschine*, or "running machine," it lacked pedals and drive mechanisms, but it proved that a person could balance and steer a two-wheeled vehicle at a speed faster than walking. Drais's design spread quickly across Europe and America, where it was dubbed the "hobby horse" or "dandy horse," and it became a fashionable novelty among the wealthy.

The next major step came in the 1860s, when French inventors, most notably Pierre Michaux and his associates, attached pedals directly to the front wheel's axle. This created the "velocipede," which the public soon called the "boneshaker" because its iron-banded wooden wheels and rigid frame transmitted every bump to the rider. Though uncomfortable, the velocipede established the principle of human-powered rotary motion that defines the modern bicycle. Its great limitation was the front wheel: the larger it grew, the faster the machine could travel, yet the rider sat dangerously high above the ground.

This tension produced the "penny-farthing," or high-wheeler, of the 1870s and 1880s. Its enormous front wheel, sometimes more than five feet in diameter, allowed a single pedal revolution to cover great distance, but a sudden stop could send the rider headlong over the handlebars. Despite this hazard, the penny-farthing became a symbol of Victorian sporting daring, and clubs formed in Britain and the United States to race and tour on them.
